query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Ultrasonic burnishing of the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating produces a refined, near-surface microstructure that, under high-temperature sliding, favors the formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer. This combined effect increases local hardness and reduces dislocation‐mediated plastic deformation, thereby lowering both the friction coefficient and wear rate relative to an untreated (baseline) coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate produced by standard deposition methods, characterized by a relatively coarse near-surface grain structure and baseline surface roughness.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-deposition ultrasonic burnishing treatment to the coating to refine the near-surface grain structure.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., operating between approximately 673 K and 1073 K) under controlled load and sliding speed that are representative of the intended service environment.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined near-surface microstructure with an increased density of grain boundaries that facilitates the in situ formation of a thin, stable oxide layer during high-temperature sliding.
generation.mechanism: The ultrasonic burnishing treatment creates finer grains in the coating’s near-surface region, which enhances dislocation pinning and surface hardness. At high temperatures, these refined boundaries promote the rapid and uniform formation of a protective oxide film. This film, together with the higher hardness, mitigates both adhesive and abrasive wear by limiting plastic flow and micro-cracking during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline untreated coating, the burnished coating will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and a reduced wear rate. Microstructural analyses will reveal fewer and smaller deformation features (e.g., micro-cracks and localized plastic flow) as well as a more uniform, adherent oxide layer forming on the surface during high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: The standard FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating prepared without ultrasonic burnishing.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding regimes (approx. 673–1073 K) where oxidation and dynamic recovery processes are active; the effects at room temperature or under very different sliding loads may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative changes in friction and wear rates are not predicted precisely due to limited specific data on the burnished FeNiCrCoCu system at high temperatures. There is also some uncertainty about the interaction between grain refinement and oxide formation kinetics under service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on identical metal substrates: one set remains as-deposited (baseline) and the other undergoes ultrasonic burnishing. Subject both sets to controlled, identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., at approximately 800°C) under the same load and sliding speed conditions.
measurements: Obtain friction coefficient vs. sliding cycle data
Quantify wear rate via mass loss or wear scar volume measurements
Conduct microstructural analysis (SEM or TEM) to assess near-surface grain size and oxide layer characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrasonic burnished coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate, and if microstructural analysis does not reveal a refined grain structure and enhanced oxide layer formation compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Friction and wear performance tests were conducted on the substrate sample, as well as those coating samples after turning and UB treatment by an RTEC multifunctional friction and wear tester at room temperature, with a friction way of linear reciprocating motion. Before the test, the sample surface was slightly polished to make the surface smooth without an oxide layer. The counter pair was the GCr15 steel ball with a 7 mm diameter and 60 HRC. The load was 10 N, and the one-way friction distance was 4.5 mm. Furthermore, the reciprocating frequency was 2 Hz, and the friction and wear experiments hold for 15 min. The wear morphology and chemical composition were analyzed and tested by SEM and EDS. Meanwhile, a 3D Super Depth Digital Microscope (VHX-5000 KEYENCE CORPORATION, Osaka, Japan) was used to measure the wear profiles and calculate the wear loss in all testing cases.
